children: Spain’s financial intelligence unit will soon be able to freeze crypto asset accounts for up to five business days, and block individual transfers for up to ten without waiting for a court order.

Under Royal Decree-Law 44/2026, published on 25 November, Spanish anti-money laundering watchdog Sepblac is granted direct authority to lock down digital asset accounts along with traditional bank and payment accounts. Judicial oversight only required if prosecutors seek to extend a freeze beyond the initial statutory window.
However, the decree-law remains provisional until Spain’s Congress validates or rejects it within 30 days of its adoption.
Accounts and Individual Transactions Have Different Limits

The new Article 46 bis allows Sepblac, Spain’s financial intelligence unit, to suspend the use of a bank, payment or cryptoasset account when it finds indications that the account may be connected to money laundering or terrorist financing.

It can also suspend the broader business relationship between a customer and a financial services provider. An account or business-relationship restriction can remain in place for a maximum of five business days.

A separate limit applies to an individual transaction already in progress: Sepblac can stop or refuse it for up to ten business days. Both measures must end earlier if Sepblac determines that they are no longer necessary.
Once the relevant deadline expires, the restriction automatically lapses unless a court ratifies or extends it following a request submitted by a public prosecutor before the deadline.
Sepblac can issue the initial order itself, while the judicial involvement becomes necessary if authorities want to keep the restriction in place beyond the statutory limit.
Crypto Platforms Must Be Able to Execute the Orders
Cryptoasset service providers already fall within the group of businesses subject to Spain’s main AML law.

The amendment gives this existing obligation a more immediate operational consequence: covered platforms must be able to execute and subsequently lift Sepblac orders within the applicable five- or ten-day window.

Failure to comply with a suspension order will be classified as a very serious infringement. The decree also protects firms from liability when they restrict an account or transaction in accordance with Sepblac’s instructions.
The Spanish government linked the change to Financial Action Task Force standards requiring financial intelligence units to have effective powers to stop suspicious transactions.

Sepblac may also use the mechanism at the request of Spanish law enforcement or another financial intelligence unit in the EU or a third country, extending its relevance to cross-border investigations.

title: Freeze First, Court Later: Spain Lets AML Unit Halt Crypto Accounts Without a Judge
